what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: The EU's new Product Liability Directive makes software, including SaaS, a product; narrow claims, but unpatched flaws lose their defence.
sections.para: Directive 2024/2853 covers software however supplied, for products placed on the market after 9 December 2026. Missing security updates within the maker's control are no defence, attackers do not reduce liability, and EULAs cannot exclude it. Only natural persons can claim, for injury, private property or private data destroyed. For php2shell, PHP is out; unpatched vendors and SaaS likely in.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Software and SaaS are products; updates count; only people can claim, for narrow damages.
sections.para: Software is a product however supplied. A lack of needed updates is no defence while the maker controls the product, exploits do not reduce liability and contracts cannot exclude it. Only natural persons claim, for injury, private property and private data destroyed; leaks and company losses are not covered. Patching does not pull old products into scope.

sections.label: Why I read it
sections.line: A LinkedIn card prompted a reading of the directive's articles and recitals, tested against php2shell.
sections.para: Lauren Zabierek's card summarises the directive accurately. The articles name software and digital manufacturing files; SaaS and AI systems appear in the recitals. It applies to products placed on the market after, not from, 9 December 2026. This is an engineer's reading, not legal advice.

sections.label: What the articles say
sections.line: Software is a product; only people claim for limited damage; cybersecurity counts; update failures lose the defence.
sections.para: Article 4 and recital 13 make software a product however supplied, excluding information, mere source code and services as such. It covers products placed after 9 December 2026, excludes non-commercial open source, limits claims to natural persons and specific damages, and judges defects with cybersecurity requirements. Evidence disclosure and presumptions ease proof; Article 11(2) removes the later-defect defence for missing updates.

sections.label: php2shell, under the new rules
sections.line: Under the new rules, PHP itself is out; unpatched vendors and SaaS harming consumers are likely liable.
sections.para: The fix shipped on 21 October 2026; NCSC-NL tracks 674 PHP products, 206 marked vulnerable. Today's products fall under the old directive. Hypothetically, a vendor or SaaS leaving the flaw unpatched is likely liable for consumers' injury, property or wiped data, but not for data theft or business losses. Shipping on end-of-life PHP 7.4 loses the state-of-knowledge defence.

sections.label: Will it stop companies updating?
sections.line: The perverse incentive not to update is weaker than feared: patches are rarely substantial modifications.
sections.para: A substantial modification changes the product's original performance, purpose or type and increases the hazard, which a security patch does not. For new products, not updating is no defence. The directive imposes no duty to update, and shutting a product down does not erase claims, which run for 10 years.

sections.label: The questions it leaves
sections.line: Open questions: when SaaS is placed on the market, product versus service, end of support, and the CRA.
sections.para: It is unclear when continuously updated SaaS is placed on the market, where products end and services begin, who manufactures a self-hosted site, and whether ending update capability ends liability. The CRA's reporting applies from September 2026 and the rest from December 2027 but excludes standalone SaaS, which this directive includes. Business losses stay outside.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: A reading of the text, not legal advice; the php2shell cases are hypothetical; the post is quoted from its card.
sections.para: Member states transpose the directive by 9 December 2026 and courts will interpret it. Today's products fall under the old directive. Only the card in the screenshot is quoted; the rest of the post needs a sign-in.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Lauren Zabierek's post, the directive and the CRA on EUR-Lex, and the PHP site's data.
sections.para: The LinkedIn post and comments; the editor's memo; Directive (EU) 2024/2853 and Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, read on EUR-Lex on 25 October 2026; the PHP story site's data at v0.22.2; and related newsroom articles.
